reading.s: Serotonin syndrome comes from too much serotonin, so I'd stop anything suspected of adding more (serotonergic substances).
reading.why: the reason first, then what to do, the term after its plain words, as in your step 5

reading.s: No more MDMA or other stimulants, of course, but also no DXM cough syrup, the painkiller tramadol or the antibiotic linezolid.
reading.why: the obvious ones first, then "but also" the ones people don't think of, each said with what it is

reading.s: Even if they take an antidepressant every day (an SSRI like Prozac, or an SNRI or MAOI), I'd skip it until a doctor says to restart it, since missing a dose is much less risky than more serotonin right now.
reading.why: it answers the reader's worry about stopping a daily medicine, but the bracket of kinds may read like a list dropped in

reading.s: If they drank ayahuasca or another harmala brew, like Syrian rue, no more of that either, since those work the way MAOIs do.
reading.why: it starts from what the reader may be facing (they drank ayahuasca), then what to do and why

reading.s: And check whether they take supplements people don't think of as drugs, like 5-HTP, St John's wort or SAM-e.
reading.why: something to do, ending on what's in their own cupboard

reading.s: When you call medics, ask for an ambulance, since the person can get worse fast, with seizures or dangerous overheating.
reading.why: the act the line before asked for, with why an ambulance

reading.s: It may seem faster to drive them to the ER yourself, but don't: paramedics can start treating them right there, and if they have a seizure in your car, you can't help them and drive at the same time.
reading.why: the urge first (it may seem faster), then what can actually happen, pictured (a seizure in your car)

reading.s: Poison control can't treat serotonin syndrome, but if you don't know what was mixed, they can help work that out once the ambulance is on its way.
reading.why: the limit comes first ("can't treat"), which may read as a correction before the help it gives

reading.s: Their twitching and tense muscles are making a lot of heat, and overheating is the most dangerous part of serotonin syndrome, so while you wait for the ambulance, I'd get them somewhere cool, take off their extra clothes, and set a fan blowing over cool damp cloths on their skin.
reading.why: the reason and three acts in one long sentence; I joined them your way, but it may read packed

reading.s: If they still feel hot, ice packs wrapped in cloth help most at the neck, armpits and groin.
reading.why: the next step only if needed, with where the packs help most

reading.s: A cold bath would cool them faster, but if they're confused, seizing or very weak, they could slip under or breathe in water, so don't put them in one.
reading.why: it argues the rule in three clauses (would, but if, so don't), and that build read AI in the last check

reading.s: And don't count on fever reducers like Tylenol or ibuprofen, which do not help with heat generated by muscles.
reading.why: what the reader reaches for, and why it won't work, in one plain line

reading.s: The ER doctors will want to know exactly what they took, so before the ambulance comes, I'd gather their pill bottles and packages.
reading.why: why first (the ER doctors will want to know), then the act

reading.s: I'd also jot down how much of each and when, street drugs and supplements included.
reading.why: the next thing to write down, in plain words ("jot down", "street drugs")

reading.s: If they raised the dose of anything lately, note that too, since a bigger dose alone can set off serotonin syndrome.
reading.why: one detail to note, with why it matters

reading.s: And if you have a thermometer or a blood pressure cuff, take readings every so often and write them down with the time, so the doctors can see whether things are getting better or worse.
reading.why: what they can measure with what they may have at home, and what the doctors get from it
